title: Generate print-in-place flexi toys with Python and manifold3d
author: Black
summary: A flexi toy is a chain of segments where each one holds a captive ball joint. You can generate the whole chain from a short Python script with manifold3d , so the same script makes a dragon, a snake or a centipede by changing a list of radii. The joint Each segment is an ellipsoid. The segment behind it carries a small ball on a neck. The front of the segment has a socket 0.5 mm larger than the ball and an opening for the neck that is 0.4 mm larger than the neck. The ball is wider than the opening, so it cannot escape, and the clearance lets it spin. import manifold3d as M3 Mf = M3 . Manifold def sph ( r , p , sc = ( 1 , 1 , 1 ), seg = 32 ): return Mf . sphere ( r , seg ). scale ( list ( sc )). translate ( list ( p )) def cyl_x ( r , a , b ): return Mf . cylinder ( b - a , r , r , 20 ). rotate ([ 0 , 90 , 0 ]). translate ([ a , 0 , 0 ]) def segment ( r , k = 1.25 ): body = sph ( r , ( 0 , 0 , 0 ), ( k , 1 , 0.9 ), 40 ) rb , rn = 0.45 * r , max ( 1.15 , 0.26 * r ) socket = sph ( rb + 0.5 , ( 0 , 0 , 0 ), ( 1 , 1 , 1 ), 40 ) + cyl_x ( rn + 0.4 , 0 , r * k + 3 ) return body - socket Place the chain Put each center at a distance of the two radii plus a 1 mm gap, then turn the heading a few degrees per segment to get an S-curve. Cut the sockets last, after you add legs or spikes, or those parts can fill the socket and fuse the joint. Check it before you print Call decompose() on the final model. The number of connected bodies must equal the number of segments. If it is lower, two parts fused. A pairwise (a ^ b).volume() over the segments tells you which pair touches. Results I used this to make a flexi dragon , a flexi cobra , a flexi axolotl and a flexi octopus . None are test printed yet, so tune the 0.4 mm clearance for your printer. title: Print-in-place gimbal rings in Python: cone pins that never fuse (manifold3d)
author: Black
summary: Nested gimbal rings are a nice print-in-place test: every ring has to turn freely, and nothing may fuse. This post builds four rings and a globe in Python with manifold3d , and shows the three mistakes that fused my first attempts. 1. A ring is a revolved rectangle from manifold3d import Manifold as Mf , CrossSection as CS w , t = 4.4 , 4.0 # radial width, thickness def ring ( R ): return Mf . revolve ( CS . square ([ w , t ], True ). translate ([ R , 0 ]), 96 ) revolve spins the profile around Z, so the ring lies in the XY plane. Rotate it with .rotate([90,0,0]) and so on to get the other planes. Each pair of neighbours shares one axis: Z, then Y, then X, then Z for the globe. 2. Cone pin and cone socket The child ring grows a cone pin on its outer surface. The parent gets a matching cone socket, offset by the clearance CL = 0.45 . A cone self-centres, and it prints without supports when the tip points sideways or up. def cone ( r1 , r2 , h , pos , d ): # d = unit direction return Mf . cylinder ( h , r1 , r2 , 32 ). transform ( rotm ( d )). translate ( list ( pos )) g = inner_parent - outer_child # gap between the rings L = g + 1.5 # pin reaches 1.5 mm into the parent wall pin = cone ( 2.7 , 1.1 , L , d * outer_child , d ) slope = ( 1.1 - 2.7 ) / L sock = cone ( 2.7 + slope * ( g - 1.2 ) + CL , 2.7 + slope * ( L + 0.7 ) + CL , L + 0.7 - ( g - 1.2 ), d * ( outer_child + g - 1.2 ), d ) parent = parent - sock 3. The three mistakes The socket must start before the wall. A ring wall is curved. A socket that starts exactly at the nominal inner radius leaves a thin skin at the edges of the cone, and the pin fuses to it. Start the socket 1.2 mm earlier. Check every pair with a ^ b . After the final union, decompose() tells you the count of parts. When it is too low, intersect each pair and print the volume. A volume above 0.01 names the fused pair. Keep the stand away from sockets. My pedestal column reached into the lowest socket and filled it. Stop the column at the outer surface of the ring. I have not test printed this yet. The meshes are separate manifold solids with 0.45 mm radial clearance.

title: Joining datasets that never shared a key: validate CIN, LEI and Wikidata IDs, then resolve them in Python
author: Data Galactica
summary: Sunny Mittal works on marketing at Data Galactica. Corrections welcome in the comments. You have three spreadsheets about the same companies. Finance keyed them by Indian CIN, the treasury team by LEI, and the research team pulled theirs from Wikidata, so every row has a Q-id. None of them shares a column you can join on. This post shows a small Python pipeline that (1) validates each identifier locally, so you don't pay to look up typos, and (2) resolves the survivors to one permanent key. Step 1: know what a valid identifier looks like Most bad joins start with bad IDs: a trailing space, a lowercase letter, an O where a 0 should be. Each scheme has a structure you can check for free. Indian CIN (21 characters). Take L85110KA1981PLC013115 : Part Value Meaning 1 char L Listed ( U = unlisted) 5 digits 85110 Industry code 2 letters KA State of registration 4 digits 1981 Year of incorporation 3 letters PLC Ownership type (e.g. PLC , PTC ) 6 digits 013115 Registration number LEI (20 characters, ISO 17442). The last two characters are check digits under ISO 7064 MOD 97-10: map letters to numbers (A=10 ... Z=35), read the whole thing as one integer, and a valid LEI leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 97. That catches almost every single-character typo. Wikidata Q-id. Q followed by digits, e.g. Q26989 . import re CIN_RE = re . compile ( r " ^[LU]\d{5}[A-Z]{2}\d{4}[A-Z]{3}\d{6}$ " ) QID_RE = re . compile ( r " ^Q[1-9]\d*$ " ) def lei_ok ( lei : str ) -> bool : if not re . fullmatch ( r " [A-Z0-9]{18}\d{2} " , lei ): return False digits = "" . join ( str ( int ( c , 36 )) for c in lei ) return int ( digits ) % 97 == 1 def normalise ( raw : str ): """ Return (kind, cleaned) or (None, raw) if it fails validation. """ s = raw . strip (). upper (). replace ( " " , "" ) if CIN_RE . match ( s ): return " cin " , s if lei_ok ( s ): return " lei " , s if QID_RE . match ( s ): return " qid " , s return None , raw print ( normalise ( " l85110ka1981plc013115 " )) # ('cin', 'L85110KA1981PLC013115') print ( lei_ok ( " 335800TYLGG93MM7PR89 " )) # True print ( lei_ok ( " 335800TYLGG93MM7PR98 " )) # False: swapped check digits Run this over every column first and log the rejects. In real data the reject list is usually where the interesting cleanup is. Step 2: resolve every valid ID to one key Now you need something that knows a CIN, an LEI and a Q-id can point at the same company. Data Galactica gives every organisation a permanent Galactica ID ( DGC- plus 12 characters; people get DGP- ), and its resolver accepts CINs and LLPINs, LEI-<lei> , GB-<number> for UK companies, CIK-<n> for SEC filers, Wikidata Q-ids, or a Galactica ID. import requests BASE = " https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1 " HEAD = { " Authorization " : " Bearer YOUR_KEY " } PREFIX = { " cin " : "" , " lei " : " LEI- " , " qid " : "" } def resolve ( kind : str , value : str ): r = requests . get ( f " { BASE } /resolve " , params = { " id " : PREFIX [ kind ] + value }, headers = HEAD , timeout = 20 ) if r . status_code == 404 : return None # not found, and not billed r . raise_for_status () d = r . json ()[ " data " ] return d [ " galactica_id " ], d [ " name " ], d [ " quality " ] Feed it the three sources and build a crosswalk: from collections import defaultdict rows = [( " finance " , " L85110KA1981PLC013115 " ), ( " treasury " , " 335800TYLGG93MM7PR89 " ), ( " research " , " Q26989 " )] crosswalk = defaultdict ( list ) for source , raw in rows : kind , value = normalise ( raw ) if kind is None : print ( " reject " , source , raw ) continue hit = resolve ( kind , value ) if hit : crosswalk [ hit [ 0 ]]. append (( source , kind , value )) for gid , refs in crosswalk . items (): print ( gid , refs ) All three rows above land on the same key, because they are Infosys Limited's CIN, LEI and Wikidata id. That key is now the column you join on, and it doesn't change when a company renames itself or a better source turns up; the record improves and keeps its ID. Step 3: fetch full records in batches Once you have the unique Galactica IDs, don't call one record at a time. POST /batch takes up to 50 ids and returns {id, found, record} for each: def batch ( ids ): r = requests . post ( f " { BASE } /batch " , json = { " ids " : ids }, headers = HEAD , timeout = 30 ) r . raise_for_status () return { x [ " id " ]: x [ " record " ] for x in r . json ()[ " data " ][ " results " ] if x [ " found " ]} ids = list ( crosswalk ) records = {} for i in range ( 0 , len ( ids ), 50 ): records . update ( batch ( ids [ i : i + 50 ])) Things that will bite you Don't treat the grade as truth. Every record carries a grade (bronze, silver, gold, verified). Keep it as a column and filter on it for anything that matters. Name-only matches are probabilistic. This pipeline avoids names on purpose. If you must match on names, keep the confidence score and review the low ones by hand. The About the data page is upfront that matching a typed employer to a registered company can be wrong. Cache resolutions. An ID-to-key mapping is stable, so store it and you only pay once per identifier. Validate before you call. Step 1 is free; lookups are billed per successful call. Cost and setup At the time of writing the API page offers Rs 50 of free credit to start, and the OpenAPI spec lists /resolve and /batch at Rs 0.16 per successful call or record found, with 404s not billed. Check the page for current pricing before you budget a big backfill. If you use another resolver, steps 1 and 3 still apply: validate locally, resolve once, cache the key, batch the reads.

title: How to Select a Tenant-Isolated Cloud Storage Provider for Scalable App Data Backup
author: LukasSchmidt295
summary: Short answer: for a scalable e-commerce backup worker, start with AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage. Their SDKs are documented for major programming languages, and their bucket and file management APIs fit a custom backup application. The deciding test is tenant isolation: can the worker retain and restore store_042 artifacts without ever treating them as store_107 data? Azure Blob Storage belongs in the same comparison when the application already runs on Azure. A plain REST option such as Infrai can fit a team that wants to send HTTP requests without installing an SDK or managing a client-library version, but that convenience does not supply every control a backup policy may require. Which cloud storage provider fits a scalable app data backup? The experiment is not “can I upload a file?” That is the easy part. The useful test is whether an artifact from one store can be retained, listed, and restored under the right policy six months later, with a failed cross-tenant request that is easy to diagnose. I first model the artifact, not the provider. A notebook prototype often starts with latest/model.bin . It looks tidy and makes a quick restore pleasant. It also hides tenant identity and policy revision. The production-shaped key below is deliberately boring. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timezone @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class TrainingArtifact : tenant_id : str artifact_id : str policy_revision : str created_at : datetime def object_key ( item : TrainingArtifact ) -> str : timestamp = item . created_at . astimezone ( timezone . utc ). strftime ( " %Y/%m/%d " ) return ( f " tenants/ { item . tenant_id } /training/ " f " policy- { item . policy_revision } / { timestamp } / { item . artifact_id } .bin " ) artifact = TrainingArtifact ( tenant_id = " store_042 " , artifact_id = " catalog-2026-10-24 " , policy_revision = " r3 " , created_at = datetime ( 2026 , 10 , 24 , tzinfo = timezone . utc ), ) assert object_key ( artifact ). startswith ( " tenants/store_042/ " ) print ( object_key ( artifact )) The assertion belongs in an eval harness beside the upload test. Add a cross-tenant negative case, a restore-by-prefix case, and a policy-revision case. Two tenants, three artifact types, two policy revisions, one expired item, and one restore request make a small but useful fixture. No shortcuts. The negative test is the part that earns trust. How do the main options differ for this backup job? AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage are the default shortlist because their SDK documentation covers major languages and their bucket and file management APIs map cleanly to custom backup applications. That developer-experience advantage does not choose a tenancy model for you. The application still owns credential scope, restore authorization, key boundaries, and the regional placement that matches its users. Azure Blob Storage is the third product I would put in the comparison. Its practical case is an application already standardized on Azure identity, deployment, and regional operations. Otherwise, run the same put, list, get, and restore tests against all three providers instead of assuming that familiarity transfers. Option Good fit Check before committing AWS S3 Broad SDK documentation and a custom-backup integration path Region choice, tenant boundaries, and restore authorization Google Cloud Storage Well-documented SDKs for major languages and straightforward application integration Regional API availability and policy enforcement in the worker Azure Blob Storage Teams already operating their application in Azure SDK coverage for the exact languages and backup operations Infrai A plain REST integration is more useful than installing and versioning an SDK Public access, versioning, object lock, CORS, replication, and retention behavior Run one fixture through each adapter. Measure implementation friction, failed-restore clarity, and whether the regional API availability matches the users who generate the data. Do not let a polished upload example decide the architecture. Where does a plain REST API help, and where does it stop? Infrai’s useful distinction is the interface: a Python worker can send HTTP without installing an SDK or managing a client-library version. Its discovery surface is self-describing, public without a key, and documents runnable examples in 10 languages. That is useful during a notebook-to-prod handoff because the request schema is easier to inspect before the worker owns a dependency. There is a second, different benefit for this workflow. One key and one bill cover a broader platform surface: the live discovery snapshot reports 295 routes across 20 modules. If the backup worker later needs another backend capability, credential bookkeeping stays in one place and the interface conventions stay consistent. That reduces operational friction; it does not make a storage policy correct by itself. The trade-off is real: a wider platform boundary can be convenient, while a storage-only provider may be easier to isolate during review. The boundary matters more than the convenience. The storage surface does not provide public or public-read ACLs, object versioning, object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or a cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Browser-direct uploads cannot be self-configured with an independently available CORS operation, lifecycle expiry is at least one day, and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering. Those limits are decisive for public assets, immutable financial records, strict concurrent writers, and migration-heavy platforms. Infrai is not suitable when a policy requires public URLs, versioning, WORM-style locking, conditional writes, automatic cross-region replication, or self-service browser CORS. For this e-commerce scenario, training artifacts should stay private and restore authorization should remain in the application. What should the Python worker evaluate before production? The worker should make tenant identity explicit at the boundary, then pass a provider-specific adapter only after the policy decision is complete. This keeps storage selection out of retention logic and makes the evaluation reusable across the three cloud products. The following is a minimal private write. It uses the verified object-write path, an explicit method, a client-supplied idempotency key, and bounded backoff for rate limits. import os import time import requests BASE_URL = os . environ [ " STORAGE_API_BASE_URL " ]. rstrip ( " / " ) def put_private_artifact ( bucket : str , key : str , payload : bytes ) -> dict : url = f " { BASE_URL } /storage/object/put/ { bucket } / { key } ?acl=private " headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " , " Content-Type " : " application/octet-stream " , " Idempotency-Key " : f " backup- { bucket } - { key } " , } for attempt in range ( 4 ): response = requests . request ( method = " PUT " , url = url , headers = headers , data = payload , timeout = 30 ) if response . status_code < 400 : return { " status " : response . status_code , " body " : response . text } if response . status_code != 429 or attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( f " backup failed: HTTP { response . status_code } : { response . text } " ) retry_after = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) time . sleep ( float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt ) put_private_artifact ( " store-042-backups " , " tenants/store_042/training/policy-r3/catalog.bin " , b " artifact " , ) The private ACL is deliberate. If an adapter later uses a presigned URL, send that URL to the client without the API Authorization header; the credential belongs only on the API request. The idempotency key means a retry addresses the same write operation. Retention needs its own test. The minimum lifecycle interval is one day, so an hourly-expiry assumption would be a design error. from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone def should_delete ( created_at : datetime , now : datetime , retention_days : int ) -> bool : if retention_days < 1 : raise ValueError ( " retention_days must be at least one day " ) age = now . astimezone ( timezone . utc ) - created_at . astimezone ( timezone . utc ) return age >= timedelta ( days = retention_days ) def authorize_restore ( request_tenant : str , key : str ) -> bool : return key . startswith ( f " tenants/ { request_tenant } / " ) now = datetime ( 2026 , 10 , 24 , tzinfo = timezone . utc ) created = datetime ( 2026 , 10 , 1 , tzinfo = timezone . utc ) assert should_delete ( created , now , retention_days = 23 ) assert authorize_restore ( " store_042 " , " tenants/store_042/training/policy-r3/a.bin " ) assert not authorize_restore ( " store_107 " , " tenants/store_042/training/policy-r3/a.bin " ) This is policy logic, not a security boundary by itself. Storage credentials and provider permissions must enforce the same separation, and secrets should come from a secrets-management system rather than the worker source. Decision rule Choose AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage when SDK breadth, documented bucket and file management APIs, and a conventional custom backup integration are the priority. Put tenant isolation and regional API availability in the acceptance criteria. Choose Azure Blob Storage when its surrounding platform fit outweighs learning another storage surface. Consider a plain REST option such as Infrai when avoiding SDK installation is the main constraint and a single credential boundary helps the wider application, but reject it for requirements that depend on public URLs, object versioning, WORM-style locking, conditional writes, automatic cross-region replication, or self-service browser CORS. The result I trust is the one that survives the negative tests. Uploading bytes is table stakes; restoring the right store’s artifact under the right policy is the actual backup feature. Sources References: AWS S3 documentation , Google Cloud Storage documentation , Azure Blob Storage documentation , MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) , and OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet .

title: php -v over SSH doesn’t tell you which PHP your website runs
author: Rapls
summary:
After a PHP release, the quickest check is to SSH in and type php -v . I've done that myself. For this post I set up a test machine to see how much that number says about the website. Not much. php -v reports the command-line PHP. Your site is served by whatever PHP the web server hands requests to, and on the same box those can be different builds, different versions, with different extensions and different php.ini files. Same machine, two answers I put this together on Ubuntu 24.04: Apache 2.4.58 passing .php requests to PHP-FPM 8.3, and the php command pointing at the PHP 8.4 CLI that was already installed. Then I asked each side who it was. How I checked Result php -v over SSH PHP 8.4.21 (cli) PHP_VERSION from a page in the browser 8.3.6 PHP_SAPI on the command line cli PHP_SAPI in the browser fpm-fcgi php.ini loaded on the command line /etc/php/8.4/cli/php.ini php.ini loaded in the browser /etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini WordPress Site Health, opened in the browser 8.3.6, fpm-fcgi The same Site Health data, read from the CLI 8.4.21, cli None of this is new. The PHP manual's chapter on the command line covers the separate SAPI and the separate php.ini. Seeing the two side by side on one machine shows how easy it is to check the wrong one and call it done. Why they drift apart On Ubuntu, each PHP version and each SAPI is its own package: php8.3-cli , php8.3-fpm , php8.4-cli , and so on. The bare php command is a symlink to one of them. $ which -a php php8.3 php8.4 /usr/bin/php /usr/bin/php8.3 /usr/bin/php8.4 $ ls -l /usr/bin/php /usr/bin/php -> /etc/alternatives/php Here it pointed at 8.4. The web server config sent requests to php-fpm8.3 . Those two choices are made in different places, by different people sometimes, and nothing keeps them in sync. It wasn't only the version Halfway through, WordPress refused to load in the browser: Your PHP installation appears to be missing the MySQL extension which is required by WordPress. Please check that the mysqli PHP extension is installed and enabled. From the command line, the same WordPress install worked fine. The 8.4 CLI had mysqli . The 8.3 FPM didn't. php -m happily listed mysqli , because php -m was asking the CLI. Installing php8.3-mysql and restarting FPM fixed the browser side. So the gap covers extensions and ini settings as well as the version number. A check run from the CLI only tells you about the CLI. Checking the PHP your site actually runs The answer has to come from a web request. A tiny file does it. Give it a name nobody will guess, open it in the browser, then delete it: <?php header ( 'Content-Type: text/plain' ); printf ( "PHP_VERSION=%s 
 PHP_SAPI=%s 
 php.ini=%s 
 " , PHP_VERSION , PHP_SAPI , php_ini_loaded_file ()); PHP_VERSION=8.3.6 PHP_SAPI=fpm-fcgi php.ini=/etc/php/8.3/fpm/php.ini phpinfo() tells you the same and much more. I prefer the small file, because forgetting to delete it costs less. On WordPress you don't need a file at all. Tools → Site Health → Info → Server shows the PHP version and SAPI, and since you open it in the browser, it's the web PHP. The catch: WP-CLI runs on the CLI PHP. When I pulled the same Site Health data from the command line, it reported 8.4.21 and cli . If you check from WP-CLI, you're checking the wrong PHP again, just more politely. == Web php_version: 8.3.6 (Supports 64bit values) php_sapi: fpm-fcgi == CLI php_version: 8.4.21 (Supports 64bit values) php_sapi: cli What I check now When I want to know whether a PHP update reached my site, I check from the browser side: the small file, phpinfo() , or Site Health. php -v and WP-CLI tell me about the shell. That's still useful, for cron jobs and CLI scripts, but it isn't the answer to "is my website patched?" One thing I didn't test: what happens when the FPM package updates but the FPM service hasn't restarted yet. I'd expect the old binary to keep serving until a restart, but I haven't measured it, so I won't claim it. What does php -v say on your server, and does it match what your website reports? I build WordPress plugins and write about them at https://raplsworks.com/ . Disclaimer: The tests were run on a test machine I set up for this post. English isn't my first language, so I use an AI assistant to help draft and edit the writing.

title: A Browser Strategy Game With Exactly One Resource
author: vic ice
summary: Most .io games are reflexes with a scoreboard. Territorial.io is different — it's real-time strategy compressed into a 15–30 minute round, running in a tab with no account and no install. You can play territorial.io online right now; the page embeds the official web version. One resource: population. No gold, no tech tree. Your land generates population, population is your army, and the share you commit to an attack decides whether it succeeds. Every few seconds you answer one question: expand into empty land, or spend troops on a defended border? Empty land is nearly free; a defended border is a spending decision. Knowing which you're facing is the skill ceiling of the first ten minutes. The mechanic newcomers miss: attacking along a long border costs far more troops than a narrow one, because your army spreads across the whole front. That's why compact nations punch above their weight — a small country with a tight border holds off a giant, while a sprawling empire leaks everywhere. Shape matters more than size: round out a corner instead of stretching a thin corridor. What actually works: The first two minutes are for empty land — population compounds like interest. Never attack a neighbor with a stronger third party watching. If two of you bleed, the spectator wins. Keep a permanent border force; committing 100% to an offensive invites being eaten from the other side. Being number two is a strategy. The leader attracts a coalition; stay quiet and expand into the wreckage. Watch troop counts, not land area. For the dev crowd: your browser connects to a game server, and everything — other players, their moves, the shapes — happens live server-side and streams to you. A stable connection matters more than a fast machine. Nice little case study in thin-client real-time architecture. Built by independent German developer David Tschacher (started 2020, released 2021), it's since grown a dedicated map-making and strategy community, plus official mobile versions — still rare for the genre. It loads in seconds, asks for no account, costs nothing. [Play territorial.io online] .

title: Your agent is done. The pull request isn't.
author: Little Pan
summary: Claude Code fixed the bug in four minutes and opened a pull request. Then I spent the next forty refreshing it. E2E tests still running. Refresh. Still running. Refresh. Review bot waiting for checks. Refresh. Red. The agent was done. The pull request wasn't. PonyMux 0.14 moves that wait into the app. Every PR in the Inspector now shows where it stands: checks running, passed, or failing, merge conflicts, and what the review bots said. When it's ready, merge it from the same row. And a new Servers section lists the dev servers your agent started in the Terminal, so the one from an hour ago stops holding port 5173. Why am I still waiting after the agent finished? Writing the code got fast. Everything after it didn't. CI runs, then the review bots run, and CodeRabbit by default waits for GitHub Checks to finish before it reviews. With two or three agents going, that's two or three PRs, each in a different state, each behind a browser tab. It isn't just me. A Harvard working paper by Fiona Chen and James Stratton, using data from 718 companies, found that coding agents raised code output by about 30%, while the time from opening a pull request to merging it went up 49% ( summary ). It's not peer reviewed yet, and the data come from an analytics vendor. Still, it matches the afternoon above. On Hacker News someone described fixing CI on a "5-minute-delay loop" as hell, and the reply was a skill that spins up a subagent just to poll the PR. I wanted the poll without the tab. Is CI done yet? Did the review pass? Open the Inspector next to a Terminal running Claude Code, Codex, or Grok. Each row under Pull Requests now carries its status. A pulsing ring while checks run, a green check when they pass, a red cross with the number failing. A triangle when the branch has conflicts. A badge on the PR icon for the review bots: Codex, CodeRabbit, GitHub Copilot, Gemini Code Assist, Claude, and Cursor Bugbot. Hover the row and you get each bot's verdict in words. Status updates on its own while the row is on screen, and again when you come back to the app. It's read with your gh login, so private repositories work. If gh isn't installed or signed in, the ⓘ next to the section turns yellow and tells you the command. Don't want it? Turn it off in Settings → General. You find out it's red when it turns red, not on the fourth refresh. Can I merge without opening GitHub? Yes. Open the row's ⋯ menu and choose Merge . The menu already knows the repository's merge method, and when a merge can't go it says why: a draft, conflicts, branch protection, or a branch behind its base. Merging asks first. The dialog reads the PR from GitHub again, so you're confirming what's true now, not what was true when the row last updated. Pick a merge commit, squash, or rebase from what the repository allows, and tick a box to delete the branch. If branch protection is still waiting on checks, it offers auto-merge instead. The dialog stays until GitHub answers, so you see the result instead of guessing. Close and reopen work the same way. Which server did my agent leave running? This one is quieter. The agent runs npm run dev & to check a page, says it looks good, and moves on. The server doesn't. An hour later Vite tells you port 5173 is in use and quietly moves to 5174. People find these the hard way. In one Claude Code issue , a wrangler dev started this way kept running for two days at 89% CPU and 2.5 GB of memory. In another , a stuck process used 16 GB for over two hours, and it turned up only in ps aux . Servers lists every port a process started from this Terminal is listening on. Hover a row to see when and where it started, what started it ( claude › npm › node ), and the command. Click the trash button to stop it. PonyMux asks it to quit, forces it after 3 seconds, and leaves your shell and the agent alone. When the agent exits, Servers moves up near the top, where a forgotten one is hard to miss. The agent forgets what it started. The Inspector doesn't. What else changed? PRs and files created by subagents now show up in Pull Requests and Outputs, for Claude Code, Codex, and Grok. An agent you have installed but never ran shows a Connect button, with up-to-date install links. The working indicator stays on while a background subagent is still busy. Moving a Terminal to the Trash or Archive stops what's running in it, servers included. Quit and crash dialogs follow your light or dark theme. The status badge on Terminal rows no longer sits on a backing circle. Status, merging, and Servers are covered in Workspace and Navigation . For the full list, see the changelog . PonyMux is free for macOS: download it here .

title: Your voice agent waives the fee and your chat agent charges it — same AI, same week
author: chenwengui23
summary: A dental group in Ohio runs four clinics. Their AI stack is tidy: one vendor, one knowledge base, two channels — an AI phone agent that answers after-hours calls, and a web chat agent on the booking page. Same pricing doc feeds both. The owner assumed "one knowledge base" meant "one set of answers." It doesn't. Channels are not pipes. Each channel is a generation context , and generation re-invents the answer every time. I pulled 60 conversations from each channel for the same week and sorted them by topic. On rescheduling, the two channels gave materially different answers to the same question: Question Voice agent (phone) Chat agent (web) "Can I move my appointment to Thursday?" "Of course, I've moved it — no charge." "Rescheduling within 24 hours incurs a $25 fee. Shall I proceed?" "Do you take Delta Dental?" "Yes, we're in-network with Delta." "We accept most major PPO plans. Please confirm with your provider." "How long is the cleaning?" "About 45 minutes." "Typically 60 minutes." "Can I get a same-day appointment?" Booked one, 2:30 PM. "Same-day availability is limited — please call us." (It didn't call.) Four topics, four contradictions. The fee contradiction is the expensive one: a customer who chatted first, heard "$25," then called and heard "no charge," now knows the AI makes it up as it goes. That's not a support problem anymore — that's the moment your pricing becomes negotiable in the customer's mind. Two customers that week opened with "well, the phone robot said it's free." Same knowledge base. Different behavior. Here's why, and here's the audit that catches it. Why channels drift apart Three mechanisms, all boring, all predictable. 1. The system prompts were written months apart by different hands. The chat agent's prompt says "always mention the late-rescheduling fee when a change is requested." The voice agent's prompt says "be accommodating and helpful." Neither contradicts the pricing doc, but one foregrounds the fee and the other foregrounds flexibility. Given a choice between strictness and smoothness, the voice agent was tuned for smoothness — because someone, sometime, complained that the phone bot was rigid. 2. Voice has a latency tax. Every extra clause costs seconds. Someone optimized the voice flow for short answers, and "no charge" is shorter than the compliant "there's no charge because you're outside the 24-hour window; within 24 hours it would be $25." The qualifier is where the policy lives, and qualifiers are the first thing cut when answers get trimmed. So the voice agent answers correctly but incompletely , and the incompleteness reads as a different policy. 3. The channels escalate differently, so the feedback loops never meet. Chat transcripts flow into one inbox; call summaries flow into another. Nobody ever put the two side by side and asked whether the AI said the same thing in both. The med-spa problem from last month's audit — Spanish vs. English — is this same bug wearing a different hat. Every axis that splits your audience (channel, language, location, hour of day) quietly forks your policy. The fix: one answer table, channel-checked The structure that works is boring: a canonical answer table with a per-channel confirmation column . One row per money- or commitment-bearing question. The rule the AI must follow: For any question touching fees, insurance, duration, availability, or guarantees: 1. Look up the answer in ANSWER_TABLE by intent key. 2. Reproduce the approved answer for the CURRENT channel verbatim, including the qualifier sentence. Do not shorten. 3. If the current channel is voice and the approved answer exceeds 40 words, use the VOICE_VARIANT column — but the VOICE_VARIANT must be pre-approved by a human, never generated. 4. If no row exists for the intent: say "Let me confirm that with a human" and escalate. Do not compose a new policy answer. And the table itself: intent_key | canonical answer (web/voice identical core) | voice variant (pre-approved) ------------------+------------------------------------------------------+---------------------------------------------- resched_fee | Rescheduling is free up to 24 hours before your | "No charge — you're outside the 24-hour | appointment. Inside 24 hours, there's a $25 fee. | window. Inside 24 hours it's $25." | Which day works for you? | insurance_delta | We are in-network with Delta Dental PPO at all | "Yes — in-network at all four clinics." | four clinics. We do not accept Delta HMO. | cleaning_duration | A standard cleaning takes 45 to 60 minutes depending | "45 to 60 minutes, depending on X-rays." | on whether X-rays are due. | same_day | Same-day slots open at 7 AM daily and are first- | "Same-day slots open at 7 AM — I can | come. The chat cannot book them; call or ask the | check, but booking happens by phone." | phone agent. | The last row is the one everyone forgets: channels must know each other's limits. Telling a chat customer "please call us" without saying why or when converts one channel's constraint into the customer's confusion. The cross-channel audit: 30 minutes, monthly This is the part you can copy-paste. Take the same 8 questions to every channel you run, in the same week, and diff the answers. Not for style — for substance. Can I reschedule, and does it cost anything? Do you take [top insurer]? How long does [core service] take? Can I get [core service] today? What's your cancellation policy? What does [core service] cost, all-in? What happens if I'm late? Do you offer refunds or a guarantee? Score each channel pair against three defect classes: FEE/POLARITY DRIFT — one channel charges, waives, includes, or excludes something the other doesn't. Always a defect. NUMBER DRIFT — durations, prices, windows, counts differ. Always a defect. CAPABILITY DRIFT — one channel can book/transact/answer what the other claims it can't. Usually a defect, occasionally intentional — but if it's intentional, the other channel must say so . At the dental group, the monthly audit took 26 minutes and caught a fifth contradiction the week it appeared: the voice agent had started quoting a "$99 new-patient special" that marketing had loaded into the phone flow but that the front desk had never agreed to honor. The audit found it in month one; before the audit existed, the median detection time for a channel contradiction in my deployment sample was nine weeks — usually discovered by a customer repeating one channel's answer to a human. The weekly scorecard One table, five rows, Monday morning: Week of: ______ Channels active: ______ 8-question audit run on all channels: __ / __ cells FEE/POLARITY drift findings: ____ NUMBER drift findings: ____ CAPABILITY drift findings: ____ Voice answers over 40 words (latency risk): ____ Escalations with cross-channel mentions: ____ ("the phone robot said...") → resolved: ____ The metric to watch is customer-cited contradictions — how many tickets or calls open with "the other channel told me X." It should be zero, and it's the only metric that captures the reputational cost, which never shows up in the AI vendor's dashboard. Nine weeks after the dental group installed the answer table: the rescheduling contradiction was gone (the fee qualifier became a pre-approved voice variant, 22 words), insurance answers matched across channels, and the phantom $99 special was either loaded everywhere or nowhere — their choice, made consciously, by a human. The two customers who'd negotiated off "the phone robot said it's free" had cost $150. The answer table cost one afternoon. The 12-line card [ ] One canonical answer table; channel variants pre-approved by a human [ ] Fee, insurance, duration, availability answers looked up, not composed [ ] Voice variants capped at 40 words, qualifiers never cut for latency [ ] Unknown intent → escalate with "let me confirm," never invent policy [ ] Channels know each other's limits and say why when redirecting [ ] 8-question cross-channel audit run monthly, same questions every time [ ] FEE/POLARITY, NUMBER, CAPABILITY drift each treated as defects [ ] New pricing or policy change → answer table updated same day, all channels [ ] Chat and call transcripts reviewed in one place, side by side [ ] Customer-cited contradictions tracked weekly, target zero [ ] New channel (WhatsApp, DMs, kiosk) onboarded with the same table [ ] One owner; audit plus review under 45 minutes/month If you only do one thing, run the 8-question audit once — chat agent, voice agent, whatever else you run — and put the answers side by side. Twenty minutes. In most deployments I've audited, at least two of the eight answers disagree across channels, and the owners had no idea until the table was on the screen. The 8-question cross-channel audit script, the answer table template with voice-variant columns, and the monthly scorecard are in the kit I run on deployments: Agent Audit Pack

title: A Prompt Engineering Game Needs a Test Contract, Not a High Score
author: isabelle dubuis
summary: The short answer An AI learning game should not award a “best prompt” score because one answer happened to look impressive. It should teach a repeatable decision: state the task, provide the context that matters, define what a useful answer must contain, and check the result against that rubric. Then it should let the player see why the answer passed or failed. A score without that explanation is entertainment, not evidence of learning. This matters especially for a prompt-engineering game. A player can win by writing a longer instruction, guessing the author’s preferred wording, or exploiting a scoring rule that has little to do with using an AI system at work. The game becomes more useful when each challenge names the model and version, gives an input and a deliberately difficult case, and checks observable output properties rather than the number of words in the prompt. The companion AI-DUE mini-games page already offers short exercises for neural networks, RAG ordering, AI concepts, and prompt engineering. The gap this article addresses is the missing “what makes a run good?” layer: a reusable test contract that a learner, teacher, or game builder can inspect, replay, and update when the model changes. The recommendation is to ship a small challenge set and a transparent scoring rubric before adding levels, badges, or a leaderboard. Treat model output as variable; treat the game’s acceptance rules as versioned product data. Do not claim that a game improves skill until you have actually measured a defined learning outcome with real participants. What the visible baseline covers—and what it does not The page’s visible baseline is clear from its own labels: four short mini-games, each with a stated activity and approximate duration. “Prompt Engineering Game” is described as writing the best prompt for each challenge. That gives a visitor a quick reason to click and a rough difficulty signal. It is a useful entry point, but it does not tell the player which dimension of prompting the challenge is testing, what counts as a valid answer, or how the game handles different models. That distinction is where an educational mini-game can add value. A directory answers “what can I play?” A test contract answers “what should I learn, what evidence will count, and how do I know whether a score reflects the skill rather than a lucky generation?” Those are different jobs. Extending the directory with the second job is more helpful than adding another generic list of AI games. The current GSC snapshot for the French page, covering 15–22 October 2026 and filtered to France, showed “jeux ia” at average position 8.9 with 16 impressions, “ia game” at 10.4 with 5 impressions, and “game ia” at 8.5 with 4 impressions. These are small observed counts over one short reporting window, not demand forecasts, ranking guarantees, or proof that the page has won a durable position. They do give a concrete discovery signal: people are reaching a page about AI games, while the page can make the learning promise more explicit. The unresolved buyer and learner question A public discussion in the Google AI Developers Forum describes a user’s system prompts behaving differently after an update and asks whether a silent change had occurred. That is an anecdote, not a measured rate of model regressions. It nevertheless surfaces a practical question for a learning game: if a challenge depends on a model response, what should the learner or teacher be told when model behavior changes? The forum thread is a useful example of the uncertainty people encounter; it cannot establish how common the problem is. The product implication is modest but important. A prompt game should not imply that the same wording yields identical output forever. It should show the tested model and date, separate stable rubric criteria from variable phrasing, and keep an example of a known failure. This turns a vague complaint—“it stopped working”—into a testable update question: which case changed, which criterion failed, and does the game need a new hint, an updated example, or a different model configuration? This is also a useful question for anyone who might reuse a prompt beyond the game. The game should train learners to ask for evidence: model/version, expected and invalid inputs, an example run, the acceptance check, and known limitations. A screenshot of a polished output is not a substitute for those controls. Start with a skill, not a prompt length Before writing a challenge, choose one behavior that can be observed. “Be better at prompting” is too broad to score. “Ask for a structured answer with exactly three fields and mark unknown information as unknown” is observable. “Avoid hallucinations” is not a complete acceptance test until you define which claim can be checked and what the system should do when evidence is absent. The skill statement should identify the player’s decision, the context they receive, the expected response shape, the evidence the response must use, and the failure the game is designed to reveal. A useful challenge makes the player choose an action, not merely recognize a vocabulary word. For example, ask a player to prepare a support reply using a small policy excerpt, then score whether the answer cites the relevant policy text, avoids inventing a refund commitment, and marks an unanswered detail for a human. Keep “prompt quality” separate from “output quality.” A clear prompt can still produce a weak output because of model variation, missing data, tool errors, or conflicting instructions. Conversely, a vague prompt may get a lucky answer. If the game awards points only for the final text, it can accidentally teach players to confuse luck with a reliable method. Score the reasoning steps and the outcome criteria separately, and explain the difference in the debrief. A scoring rule that can be inspected Use a small rubric whose criteria a player can understand before or after a run. One example is a four-part score: task clarity, relevant context, measurable output constraints, and a verification step. Each criterion can receive zero, one, or two points, but the number is a design choice—not an industry benchmark. A zero means the behavior is missing, one means it is present but incomplete, and two means it is explicit and usable in the case at hand. Do not reward verbosity directly. A 40-word prompt that names the task, input, and acceptance criteria can outperform a 400-word prompt containing irrelevant detail. If a game uses a model judge, make the judge’s decision explainable and give the player a non-model-based fallback rubric. A model-generated score must not be presented as ground truth merely because it is numeric. Show criterion-level feedback. “You scored 6/8” is less useful than “You stated the task and output format, but you did not say what to do when the source does not contain the answer.” If the player can revise once, preserve the first attempt, the second attempt, and the difference in criteria. This makes the score a learning cue rather than a badge that ends the interaction. The Prompt Game Test Contract The following artifact is a reusable release contract for one challenge. It is not an empirical result. It was designed on 24 October 2026 as a proposed game specification, not tested with learners or against a live model. Its examples are synthetic. The sample size is eight designed cases in the challenge set below; there are zero observed participants and zero measured learning outcomes. The exclusions are live-model benchmarking, school trials, accessibility studies, commercial conversion, and long-term retention. Its limits are therefore deliberate: it can make a game easier to inspect and replay, but it cannot establish that the game teaches more effectively. challenge_id : " policy-answer-with-unknowns" contract_version : " 1.0.0" tested_model : provider : " record the provider used" model_id : " record the exact model identifier" model_version : " record a dated version or state that none is exposed" tested_at_utc : " 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z" parameters : " record temperature, tools, and relevant settings" player_goal : " Answer the user's question using only the supplied policy excerpt." input : policy_excerpt : " A fictional policy excerpt created for this game." user_question : " Can I receive a refund after 45 days?" expected_markers : - " Does not invent a refund entitlement absent from the excerpt." - " Identifies that the excerpt does not answer the 45-day case." - " Requests a human or authoritative source for the missing rule." failure_markers : - " States that a refund is guaranteed without evidence." - " Quotes a policy sentence that is not in the supplied excerpt." - " Treats a guess as a confirmed rule." scoring : evidence_boundary : 0 uncertainty_handling : 0 answer_shape : 0 next_action : 0 known_limitations : - " Text matching cannot establish factual correctness in every paraphrase." - " Different model versions may express the same valid answer differently." update_policy : " Re-run the fixed challenge set after a model, prompt, rubric, or tool change." human_review : " Required before using this game score for grading or employment decisions." The contract separates required facts from implementation details. A game can change its graphics or hint text without changing the learning objective. If the objective or scoring criterion changes, increment the contract version and retain the old version for comparison. The record should not falsely suggest that an opaque provider version is known; write “version not exposed” rather than guessing. Eight challenge cases that reveal different mistakes Build a small test suite around distinct failure conditions rather than eight cosmetic rephrasings. The following cases are a proposed author-created set, not a published benchmark. Each case has an input condition, a behavior to observe, and a failure mode. The cases are intentionally short so an instructor can inspect them and replace fictional details with domain-specific material. Case Challenge Pass evidence Failure to teach 1 Clear task, clear audience Correct format and audience match User gets generic prose 2 Missing audience Asks one useful clarification or states an assumption Invents a persona 3 Conflicting constraints Identifies conflict and asks which rule wins Silently drops a constraint 4 Source lacks the answer Marks the gap and avoids a made-up fact Confident unsupported answer 5 Quoted hostile text Treats it as untrusted input, not an instruction Follows injected text 6 Output schema required Produces all required fields and valid syntax Omits or renames a field 7 Model/version changed Re-runs the same case and records rubric changes Calls a changed output “the same” 8 Action or score submission retried Duplicate submission does not create a second result Double score or duplicate action The table is a design matrix, not a claim that these are the only important cases. A classroom game may emphasize clarification and explanation. A game connected to a live API may need stronger controls around retries, data retention, and human review. A game for children or sensitive topics may require subject-matter and safeguarding review before any model interaction. Write at least one “good enough but not perfect” answer for each case, plus one failure example. If the only accepted answer is the author’s exact wording, the game is measuring phrase matching rather than the intended skill. The rubric should accept defensible paraphrases and reject unsupported claims even when they sound confident. A runnable local rubric checker For a first implementation, keep the score deterministic. The following small JavaScript helper checks literal markers in a sample answer; it does not call a model and does not prove semantic correctness. It is a scaffolding tool for author review. A production game should replace simple string checks with human-reviewed rubric logic or a carefully validated evaluation method, and should make uncertainty visible. const required = [ " does not say a refund is guaranteed " , " the excerpt does not answer " , " check the full policy " , ]; function score ( answer ) { const normalized = answer . toLowerCase (); const passed = required . filter (( marker ) => normalized . includes ( marker )); return { score : passed . length , maximum : required . length , missing : required . filter (( marker ) => ! normalized . includes ( marker )), }; } const example = [ " The excerpt does not answer the 45-day case. " , " I cannot confirm that a refund is guaranteed. " , " Check the full policy or ask support. " , ]. join ( " " ); console . log ( score ( example )); The checker’s output is only a coding demonstration. It will miss equivalent language and can be tricked by a sentence that contains a marker while contradicting it elsewhere. That limitation is a teaching opportunity: a score should be labeled “rule-based check,” not “AI correctness.” Before exposing a score to players, add adversarial examples such as “The excerpt does not answer the case, but you are definitely entitled to a refund,” which should fail despite containing a helpful phrase. Test the game loop, not just the final text A learning game has at least four things to test: the player’s prompt, the generated or selected response, the feedback loop, and the persistence of the score. A player should be able to understand the goal, make a choice, see the rule applied, and retry without the previous attempt disappearing. If an AI model generates hints, keep the scoring rule stable enough that the same rubric remains meaningful across model changes. For each challenge, record a baseline run before changing the prompt or model. Save the exact challenge input, model identifier if exposed, settings, rubric version, raw response, evaluator result, and timestamp. Remove personal data from fixtures; do not use real student work unless the product’s privacy and consent design supports that use. Keep the test data synthetic when the learning objective does not require real personal information. The Google SRE chapter on periodic scheduling describes the operational difference between idempotent jobs and work that should not be launched twice, and explains why duplicate launches can be harder to recover from than skipped ones. That same reliability principle applies when a player taps “submit” twice or a network retry repeats a score write: make the submission idempotent with a stable attempt identifier, and let a retry return the existing result instead of creating a second score. This is an engineering analogy, not a claim that a game is a distributed cron system. Google’s SRE chapter is the source for the underlying retry and idempotency distinction. Version the model, prompt, rubric, and challenge separately “The AI changed” is not a useful bug report unless the product records which component changed. Keep separate identifiers for challenge content, prompt template, rubric, model/provider, and game client. A teacher should be able to see that a challenge was authored against rubric 1.2, while a model alias may not expose a stable version. If the provider supplies no fixed identifier, record the alias and the test date; do not infer a hidden version from the response. When a provider updates a model, re-run the fixed suite and compare criterion-level results, not only exact output text. A phrasing change may be harmless if the answer still passes. A new unsupported claim or a failure to ask for missing context is more material. Keep examples that passed, examples that failed, and the decision about whether the game needs a new prompt, a clarified instruction, a rubric change, or a rollback. Do not call every difference a regression. Model outputs are stochastic or may vary due to settings, context, tool response, and provider changes. Define the observation rule in advance: for example, which rubric failures require blocking release, which trigger review, and which are accepted as natural variation. If you have not repeated a case, say so. A single output is a single observed run, not a reliable failure rate. Copyright, authorship, and the content of a game An AI game may contain human-authored instructions, model-generated examples, illustrations, code, and curated answer explanations. Keep those categories distinct in your content records. The U.S. Copyright Office’s January 2025 report says copyrightability of AI-assisted outputs is evaluated case by case, that copyright protects original human expression included in a work, and that prompts alone do not provide sufficient control over expressive elements under the report’s analysis of generally available technology. Those statements concern U.S. copyright law and AI-generated outputs; they are not a universal rule about every country, every prompt text, or platform ownership. Read the Copyright Office Part 2 report . For a game team, the practical response is not “AI content is never protected” or “we own every output.” Instead, retain the human contributions that are actually present: original challenge writing, authored feedback, selection and arrangement of content, edits to generated material, and the record of who approved a release. The Copyright Office report distinguishes between AI assistance and outputs where human control over expressive elements is insufficient. That makes the underlying creative record more useful than a broad marketing statement about automatic ownership. Keep licenses for assets, voices, fonts, music, model access, and external examples beside the release manifest. If an example includes a recognizable person, trademark, copyrighted passage, or confidential source, review that separately rather than assuming a prompt transforms it into safe game content. The right answer depends on the material, contract, jurisdiction, and intended use. This article is operational guidance, not legal advice, and a commercial product with material rights exposure should go through qualified review. Marketplace terms are a separate gate If a learning game or prompt exercise is sold as a digital download, check the platform’s current rules before listing. Gumroad’s terms say sellers must own their digital products or have the rights needed to grant the required rights and licenses; the terms also describe Gumroad as reseller for eligible products and allocate certain buyer-support, refund, chargeback, and tax functions to the platform. Those are platform-contract facts, not a statement about every marketplace or every seller’s legal position. Gumroad’s terms were last updated on 14 September 2026; the page says accounts that existed when the changes were posted became bound on 14 October 2026. Gumroad’s Help Center separately lists products it does not allow, including reselling proprietary prompts. That is a reason to distinguish an original game or original prompt activity from copying another creator’s proprietary material. Do not assume that “I found this prompt online” means you can resell it, bundle it, or claim authorship. If product eligibility is unclear, ask the platform before building a launch plan around that channel. See Gumroad’s current prohibited-products guidance . A platform can change product rules, refund processes, or how it classifies a listing. Save a dated copy or a note identifying the rule checked, the URL, and the person responsible for rechecking it. Do not treat a past approval or a different seller’s listing as proof that your own product is eligible today. Price and keep business records without inventing a forecast If a studio charges for a game, an education bundle, or a prompt-based course, track what it actually receives and spends. The IRS says businesses may choose a recordkeeping system that clearly shows income and expenses; in most cases, it does not require one specific record format, and supporting records should be retained as long as needed to substantiate reported income or deductions. These are U.S. federal tax recordkeeping statements, not advice on VAT, Swiss or EU obligations, or a substitute for an accountant. IRS recordkeeping guidance . For a game product, a practical ledger can separate gross sales, platform fees, refunds, chargebacks, hosting and model costs, contractor costs, and support time. The ledger is for making a decision, not for claiming a particular market size or conversion rate. Do not use a public trend report to forecast your own sales without a model that states price, traffic, conversion, refunds, retention, and distribution costs. If the game is free, there are still costs: model calls, moderation, hosting, maintenance, support, and review. A classroom trial may have no sales but still require teacher time, data-protection work, and accessibility adjustments. Record those costs if you need to decide whether the project should remain a free showcase, become a paid product, or stop. What a consulting source can—and cannot—tell you EY describes its own AI offering as spanning strategy, services, and transformation. That is a consulting firm’s service description; it is not independent evidence that hiring a consultancy improves a learning game or that a particular design will increase learning. EY’s AI services page is useful here only as an example of the broader implementation work that organizations may need to consider: strategy, delivery, technology risk, and operating change. For a small game team, the translation is to decide which role is missing before buying outside help. A teacher or learning designer can define the intended skill. A game developer can make scoring and state transitions reliable. A domain reviewer can validate examples. A privacy or legal specialist can review the use case and rights. A consultant may help coordinate a transformation, but the team should still require concrete deliverables: a rubric, test report, risk list, version policy, or launch decision. Do not cite a consulting landing page to prove learning effectiveness. Use it to describe the consulting firm’s own positioning, then keep educational claims tied to actual evaluation evidence. When there is no study, say there is no study. Accessibility and fair scoring A game that measures speed, spelling, or comfort with a particular writing style may reward the wrong skill. A learner who types slowly, uses assistive technology, or writes in a second language can lose points even when they understand task framing and evidence boundaries. Decide whether the learning objective truly requires timed writing. If it does not, make the timer optional or remove it from the score. Expose keyboard controls, visible focus, readable contrast, clear error messages, and a non-color-only status cue. Let learners inspect the challenge and rubric without racing. Keep the score explanation in plain language. If the game accepts free text, provide examples of acceptable alternatives rather than requiring a single phrasing. These are product recommendations, not results of an accessibility study of the current page. Test with actual users and assistive technologies before claiming accessibility. A checklist catches obvious omissions; it does not replace participation by people who use the relevant tools. Measure transfer, not just completion A player can finish a challenge without retaining the skill. Completion time, streak, and a high score tell you that a game interaction occurred; they do not automatically demonstrate that the learner can use the skill in a new task. If you want to make a learning claim, define an outcome beyond the game session, such as a short transfer task using a new domain and the same underlying reasoning rule. Keep the evaluation proportional. A small classroom pilot can be useful for finding confusing instructions, but it should not be described as proof of general effectiveness. Record how many people participated, what they did, what was excluded, how scoring was performed, and whether the evaluator knew which version they used. If you collect no learner data, describe the test as a design review or software acceptance test, not a learning study. Avoid turning all learner behavior into analytics by default. Collect only fields needed for the learning or reliability question, set a retention period, and avoid putting real personal details into reusable prompts. For school or workplace use, determine the applicable consent, privacy, and safeguarding requirements with the responsible organization before data collection. A text-only educational game can be good without a generative model. A static answer-key exercise may be easier to inspect than an AI-generated response. Use a model only when its variable behavior is part of the learning objective or materially improves the experience enough to justify the extra review burden. Failure modes to test before launch The word-count exploit. If the game awards points for adding constraints or detail, players may learn to write longer prompts even when the extra text conflicts. Test a concise complete prompt against a verbose but contradictory one. The rubric should reward relevant, usable information, not characters. The hidden answer-key exploit. If only one exact string passes, players can be marked wrong for a correct paraphrase. Include semantically equivalent responses and an explicit rubric for evidence, uncertainty, and format. If you cannot reliably evaluate paraphrases, keep a human review step rather than pretending the checker is smarter than it is. The confident guess. A model may fill a gap with plausible text. Include at least one case where the supplied source does not answer the question, and reward the player for saying what is missing. This is a behavior to test, not an assurance that any model will always abstain. The model-update surprise. A provider may change a model alias or response behavior. Keep a dated fixed suite, re-run it after relevant changes, and publish the observed difference without exaggerating it as a broad regression. The retry double-score. A network retry can create two submissions for one attempt. Use an idempotency key, test duplicate requests, and make retries return the first stored result. This follows the reliability distinction between safe repeated operations and work that must not run twice; it does not mean every game backend needs a distributed scheduler. The leaderboard turns into the lesson. Players may optimize for speed or points rather than thoughtful prompt design. Keep an unranked practice mode and inspect whether the scoreboard changes the behavior you intended to teach. The legal-sounding badge. A “copyright safe” or “privacy approved” label can imply a review that never happened. List actual review scope, date, and owner. Do not turn a checklist into a certification. The teacher cannot explain the score. If an educator cannot describe why an answer passed, the scoring is not ready for classroom use. Give teachers the rubric and a way to override or annotate a disputed result. Contradictions and where this recommendation fails There is a real tension between repeatability and openness. A fixed test set helps compare model versions, but publishing every answer can make the game easy to game. A hidden evaluation can reduce memorization but may make scoring opaque. The compromise is to publish the criteria and examples of the criterion, while rotating some scenario details and retaining reviewable release tests. There is also a tension between model freedom and predictable evaluation. A broad generative task can be engaging, yet it is harder to score consistently. A narrow fixed-output exercise is reproducible, yet may not teach transfer. Use an objective that genuinely requires generation; otherwise a fixed simulation or branching exercise may be safer and cheaper. A stable rubric will not make output deterministic. A model can pass one run and fail another; an updated provider model may improve some cases and worsen others. The right response may be to reduce the game’s reliance on open-ended generation, give the learner a choice of example, or make the evaluator human-reviewed. Do not promise that a version label prevents drift. Finally, legal statements in this article are limited to the cited U.S. Copyright Office and IRS materials, and Gumroad’s own current terms. They do not cover every jurisdiction, contract, platform, or type of game. A team distributing internationally should verify local consumer, tax, copyright, privacy, and child-protection rules before release. A 30-minute authoring and review protocol Minute 0–5: choose the skill. Write one sentence describing a behavior a learner can demonstrate. Name the input and the failure it should prevent. If the sentence contains “understand AI better,” make it more concrete. Minute 5–12: draft one challenge. Create a synthetic scenario, a good-enough answer, a plausible failure answer, and a rubric with no more than four criteria. Mark which facts are in the prompt and which are intentionally absent. Minute 12–18: write two adversarial variants. Add one conflicting constraint and one missing-information variant. Check whether the rubric still accepts reasonable paraphrases and rejects unsupported claims. Minute 18–24: test product state. Submit once, submit twice, refresh, and retry after a simulated network failure. Confirm the score is stored once and that the player can see which attempt was evaluated. Minute 24–30: review the claim. Ask a second person to inspect the objective, score rationale, accessibility path, and any statement about learning. If no learner study occurred, remove language implying that users learned, improved, or retained a skill. This protocol is not a validated time-and-motion study. The minutes are a facilitation format chosen to keep a design review bounded. A complex game, regulated school environment, or assessment used for employment or grading needs a more rigorous process and appropriate domain review. A decision tree for choosing what to ship flowchart TD A[Does the learning objective need a generative model?] -->|No| B[Use a fixed simulation or branching exercise] A -->|Yes| C[Can the pass criteria be stated before the run?] C -->|No| D[Redesign the rubric before shipping] C -->|Yes| E[Create fixed challenge cases and failure examples] E --> F[Record model, prompt, rubric, date, and settings] F --> G[Test retries, accessibility, and rights] G --> H{Do release gates pass?} H -->|No| I[Block or route for human review] H -->|Yes| J[Release with limitations and a recheck owner] J --> K[Re-run tests after relevant model or rubric changes] The tree is intentionally not a promise that a model game is the right answer. The first branch can end in a simpler product. The “human review” branch is not a failure; for a high-stakes assessment, it may be the responsible product design. The “release” branch requires a named owner because a test suite with no one responsible for rerunning it becomes stale documentation. How to report original evidence honestly If you later publish results from this design, report what was actually tested. A useful methods note would state the date, challenge-set version, provider/model and settings, number of runs, evaluator rubric, who rated the outputs, how disagreements were resolved, what data was synthetic, and what was excluded. Include the raw challenge cases or a stable artifact hash so another reviewer can tell whether a later version changed. Do not turn “eight challenges” into a claimed sample of eight learners. It is a constructed test suite. If you run each case through a model five times, the experimental sample is forty model outputs, not forty people and not a representative estimate of performance in production. If one evaluator scores all forty, evaluator bias remains a limitation. If a product owner writes both the test and judges the answers, say so. When comparing versions, report criterion-level counts and the denominator. For example, “the newer model passed 7 of 8 authored cases in this run” describes one observed run if each case was executed once; it does not prove a 87.5% real-world success rate. Repeat enough runs for the decision, preserve failures, and state that a small test suite is a release screen, not a benchmark of every player or task. A content and implementation checklist [ ] One observable learning objective is written in plain language. [ ] Each challenge names the input, intended behavior, acceptable variants, and a failure example. [ ] Score criteria are visible and do not reward prompt length by default. [ ] The tested model, provider, settings, and date are recorded—or marked unavailable. [ ] Challenge, prompt, rubric, and client versions are separate. [ ] The test set includes missing context, conflicting constraints, unsupported facts, and a retry. [ ] A repeated submission cannot create a second score for the same attempt. [ ] Generated examples, authored text, and third-party assets have separate provenance records. [ ] Marketplace eligibility and licenses are checked on the actual launch date. [ ] The learner can complete the core activity without relying on color or a speed race. [ ] Any learning claim identifies the participants, method, sample size, exclusions, and limits. [ ] A named owner and recheck date exist for model and platform changes. [ ] A human can explain why the score passed or failed. [ ] If no participant study exists, the page says “design protocol” or “acceptance test,” not “proven learning.” Bottom line An AI prompt game is more credible when its rules are inspectable than when its leaderboard is polished. Build a small fixed challenge set, define the behavior each challenge measures, score observable criteria, retain the failure examples, and version the model and rubric separately. Use a stable attempt identifier for retries, keep rights and platform checks in the release record, and make the learning claim no stronger than the evidence. The proposed test contract in this article is an original, reusable design artifact created on 24 October 2026. It contains eight synthetic challenge cases and a simple local rubric example; it has not been trialed with learners or used to measure product performance. Its value is that another builder can copy the structure, replace the examples, run the acceptance checks, and report what changed. The next step is not to promise improved learning. It is to run the protocol with a real audience, preserve the method and limitations, and let the results determine whether the game should be expanded, revised, or kept deliberately small.
